cards.q: What is the classic chest x-ray appearance of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?
cards.a: Diffuse reticulogranular ("ground-glass") opacities with air bronchograms and low lung volumes.

cards.q: What medication can accelerate fetal lung maturation when preterm delivery is anticipated?
cards.a: Antenatal corticosteroids, such as betamethasone, when indicated by gestational age and clinical circumstances.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of meconium aspiration syndrome?
cards.a: A newborn with respiratory distress, often with meconium-stained amniotic fluid, and patchy pulmonary opacities.

cards.q: What serious complication can occur with meconium aspiration?
cards.a: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).

cards.q: What is the underlying problem in persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn?
cards.a: Persistently elevated pulmonary vascular resistance causes right-to-left shunting through fetal circulatory pathways, producing hypoxemia.

cards.q: What is a characteristic finding in PPHN?
cards.a: Differential oxygen saturation between the preductal and postductal circulations may occur because of right-to-left ductal shunting.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of intussusception-associated bowel ischemia?
cards.a: Increasing abdominal pain, abdominal distention, bloody stool, systemic toxicity, and eventually peritonitis or shock.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute abdominal pain requiring surgery in children?
cards.a: Appendicitis is the most common surgical cause of acute abdominal pain in children.

cards.q: What is the classic laboratory pattern in acute appendicitis?
cards.a: Leukocytosis with neutrophilia may occur, although normal laboratory values do not exclude appendicitis.

cards.q: What is the classic ultrasound finding of appendicitis?
cards.a: A noncompressible, enlarged appendix, typically >6 mm in diameter, with associated inflammatory findings.

cards.q: What is the typical presentation of viral hepatitis A in an older child?
cards.a: Fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, followed by jaundice and dark urine.

cards.q: What laboratory pattern is characteristic of acute hepatitis?
cards.a: Markedly elevated AST and ALT, often with increased bilirubin.

cards.q: What is the major route of transmission of hepatitis A?
cards.a: Fecal-oral transmission.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute hepatitis B infection?
cards.a: It may be asymptomatic or cause fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, and elevated aminotransferases.

cards.q: Which pediatric liver disease is strongly associated with Wilson disease?
cards.a: Chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure, and neurologic disease can occur because of copper accumulation.

cards.q: What is the characteristic laboratory clue to Wilson disease?
cards.a: Low ceruloplasmin with increased tissue copper; 24-hour urinary copper is often elevated.

cards.q: What eye finding is associated with Wilson disease?
cards.a: Kayser-Fleischer rings, caused by copper deposition in the cornea.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of intussusception caused by IgA vasculitis?
cards.a: A child with palpable purpura, abdominal pain, arthralgia, and renal findings may develop intussusception due to bowel-wall edema.

cards.q: What is the classic gastrointestinal manifestation of IgA vasculitis?
cards.a: Colicky abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding due to intestinal vasculitis and edema.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Meckel diverticulum inflammation?
cards.a: It can mimic acute appendicitis, causing right lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and vomiting.

cards.q: What embryologic remnant forms Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a:
The vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct.
PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY

cards.q: What is the most common arrhythmia in children?
cards.a: Sinus tachycardia is common; among clinically significant supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, SVT is particularly important.

cards.q: What ECG finding distinguishes SVT from sinus tachycardia in a child?
cards.a: SVT often has a very rapid, regular narrow-complex rhythm with abrupt onset and termination, whereas sinus tachycardia usually has gradual onset and a normal P-wave relationship.

cards.q: What is the first treatment for a hemodynamically stable infant with SVT?
cards.a: Vagal maneuvers, followed by adenosine if the rhythm persists.

cards.q: Why should carotid sinus massage generally not be used in infants?
cards.a: It is less appropriate and potentially hazardous; safer vagal techniques such as applying a cold stimulus to the face are preferred in infants.

cards.q: What is the treatment for unstable pediatric SVT?
cards.a: Synchronized cardioversion.

cards.q: What is the classic ECG feature of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?
cards.a: Short PR interval, delta wave, and widened QRS due to ventricular preexcitation.

cards.q: What is the underlying abnormality in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?
cards.a: An accessory atrioventricular pathway bypasses the AV node.

cards.q: What is a major concern if a child with WPW develops atrial fibrillation?
cards.a: Rapid conduction through the accessory pathway can cause extremely rapid ventricular rates and potentially ventricular fibrillation.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of myocarditis progressing to dilated cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Exercise intolerance, tachypnea, hepatomegaly, edema, gallop rhythm, and other signs of congestive heart failure.

cards.q: What is the characteristic structural abnormality in dilated cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Dilated ventricular chambers with impaired systolic function.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of congestive heart failure in an infant?
cards.a: Tachypnea, feeding difficulty, diaphoresis with feeds, poor weight gain, hepatomegaly, and recurrent respiratory symptoms.

cards.q: Why do infants with heart failure often sweat during feeding?
cards.a: Feeding is an exertional activity that increases cardiac workload and sympathetic activation.

cards.q: What is a gallop rhythm in pediatric heart failure?
cards.a: An S₃ or S₄ heart sound indicating abnormal ventricular filling or compliance.

cards.q: What is the classic cause of heart failure in a young infant with a large left-to-right shunt?
cards.a: Increasing pulmonary blood flow as pulmonary vascular resistance falls after birth.

cards.q: What is the classic chest x-ray finding in significant left-to-right shunting?
cards.a: Cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings due to increased pulmonary blood flow.

cards.q: What is the physiologic reason newborns with cyanotic congenital heart disease may deteriorate after birth?
cards.a: Closure of the ductus arteriosus can eliminate a critical route for pulmonary or systemic blood flow.

cards.q: What are the major categories of ductal-dependent congenital heart disease?
cards.a: Lesions requiring the ductus for systemic blood flow or pulmonary blood flow, such as critical left-sided obstruction or severe pulmonary outflow obstruction.

cards.q: What is the classic congenital heart lesion with "single-ventricle" physiology that requires staged palliation?
cards.a: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS).

cards.q: What is the initial stabilization of a neonate with suspected HLHS?
cards.a: Prostaglandin E₁ infusion to maintain ductal patency, along with stabilization of oxygenation, ventilation, perfusion, and acid-base status.

cards.q: Why can excessive oxygen administration be problematic in certain ductal-dependent systemic lesions?
cards.a:
Oxygen can lower pulmonary vascular resistance, potentially increasing pulmonary blood flow at the expense of systemic perfusion in some lesions.
PEDIATRIC PULMONOLOGY

cards.q: What is the most common cause of wheezing in an infant?
cards.a: Viral bronchiolitis, particularly due to RSV, is a common cause.

cards.q: What is the classic auscultatory finding in bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Diffuse wheezing and crackles, often accompanied by prolonged expiration.

cards.q: Why can bronchiolitis cause feeding difficulty?
cards.a: Tachypnea and nasal congestion interfere with suck-swallow-breathe coordination.

cards.q: What is an important risk factor for severe RSV disease?
cards.a: Prematurity, especially significant prematurity, is a major risk factor; congenital heart disease and chronic lung disease also increase risk.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of airway obstruction in bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Small-airway edema, mucus production, epithelial necrosis, and cellular debris narrow the bronchioles.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of foreign-body aspiration in a toddler?
cards.a: Sudden coughing, choking, wheezing, or respiratory distress, often during eating or playing.

cards.q: What should be suspected when a previously healthy child develops sudden unilateral wheezing?
cards.a: Foreign-body aspiration until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What is the treatment for complete airway obstruction in a conscious infant?
cards.a: Five back blows followed by five chest thrusts, repeated until the obstruction is relieved or the infant becomes unresponsive.

cards.q: What is the treatment for severe foreign-body airway obstruction in a conscious child older than 1 year?
cards.a: Abdominal thrusts, repeated until the object is expelled or the child becomes unresponsive.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of an asthma exacerbation?
cards.a: Dyspnea, cough, wheezing, chest tightness, prolonged expiration, and increased work of breathing.

cards.q: What finding indicates a potentially life-threatening asthma exacerbation?
cards.a: Altered mental status, exhaustion, severe hypoxemia, rising PaCO₂, or a silent chest indicates impending or established respiratory failure.

cards.q: Why can a normal or elevated PaCO₂ be alarming during a severe asthma attack?
cards.a: A severely obstructed child initially hyperventilates and develops low PaCO₂. A normalizing or rising PaCO₂ can indicate respiratory muscle fatigue and impending respiratory failure.

cards.q: What is the expected blood-gas pattern early in a severe asthma exacerbation?
cards.a:
Respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation:

cards.q: What is the most important long-term environmental intervention for a child with asthma who is exposed to tobacco smoke?
cards.a: Eliminate exposure to tobacco smoke, including secondhand and thirdhand smoke.

cards.q: What is the major pulmonary consequence of poorly controlled persistent asthma in childhood?
cards.a: Recurrent exacerbations and airway inflammation can lead to airway remodeling and persistent impairment of lung function.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of celiac disease in a child?
cards.a: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal distention, poor weight gain, iron-deficiency anemia, and other manifestations of malabsorption after exposure to gluten.

cards.q: Which intestinal portion is primarily affected in celiac disease?
cards.a: The proximal small intestine, particularly the duodenum and jejunum.

cards.q: What histologic finding is characteristic of celiac disease?
cards.a: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

cards.q: Which antibody is preferred for initial screening of suspected celiac disease?
cards.a: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) with measurement of total IgA.

cards.q: Why should total IgA be checked when screening for celiac disease?
cards.a: Selective IgA deficiency can cause a falsely negative IgA-based celiac serology.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for celiac disease?
cards.a: A lifelong strict gluten-free diet avoiding wheat, barley, and rye.

cards.q: What nutritional deficiency is particularly common in untreated celiac disease?
cards.a: Iron deficiency, which may cause microcytic anemia.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of lactose intolerance after gastroenteritis?
cards.a: Temporary bloating, abdominal cramps, flatulence, and watery diarrhea after consuming dairy, due to secondary lactase deficiency.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of osmotic diarrhea?
cards.a: Poorly absorbed solutes remain in the intestinal lumen and retain water, increasing stool water content.

cards.q: What happens to diarrhea caused by an osmotic substance when the patient stops ingesting that substance?
cards.a: The diarrhea improves or resolves.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of secretory diarrhea?
cards.a: Large-volume watery diarrhea that persists despite fasting, caused by active intestinal secretion or impaired absorption.

cards.q: What is a common cause of secretory diarrhea in children?
cards.a: Enterotoxin-producing infections, including certain strains of E. coli.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection?
cards.a: Abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhea, typically without high fever.

cards.q: What serious complication can follow Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection?
cards.a: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).

cards.q: What are the classic features of HUS?
cards.a: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.

cards.q: What peripheral blood smear finding is characteristic of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs).

cards.q: Why should antibiotics generally be avoided in suspected STEC infection?
cards.a:
They may increase Shiga toxin release and potentially increase the risk of HUS.
PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries?
cards.a: Kawasaki disease is an important acquired cardiovascular disease of childhood.

cards.q: What laboratory findings commonly accompany Kawasaki disease?
cards.a: Elevated inflammatory markers, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis during the subacute phase, and sometimes sterile pyuria or elevated liver enzymes.

cards.q: What is the characteristic hand/foot finding in Kawasaki disease?
cards.a: Erythema and edema of the hands and feet, followed later by periungual desquamation.

cards.q: What oral finding is characteristic of Kawasaki disease?
cards.a: Strawberry tongue and erythematous, cracked lips.

cards.q: What is the preferred cardiac imaging study for monitoring Kawasaki disease?
cards.a: Echocardiography, particularly for assessing coronary artery abnormalities and ventricular function.

cards.q: What is the major long-term cardiac concern after Kawasaki disease?
cards.a: Coronary artery aneurysm and thrombosis, which can cause myocardial ischemia or infarction.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of an innocent Still murmur?
cards.a: A soft, vibratory/ musical systolic ejection murmur, usually heard along the lower left sternal border, without other abnormal cardiac findings.

cards.q: What features suggest a pathologic rather than innocent murmur?
cards.a: Diastolic murmurs, harsh or loud murmurs, holosystolic murmurs, abnormal S₂, cyanosis, syncope, abnormal pulses, or signs of heart failure.

cards.q: What is the classic murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: A harsh systolic ejection murmur that increases with decreased preload, such as during standing or Valsalva.

cards.q: Why does the murmur of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy increase with Valsalva?
cards.a: Reduced venous return decreases LV volume, bringing the hypertrophied septum closer to the mitral valve and worsening LV outflow obstruction.

cards.q: What symptom in an adolescent athlete should raise concern for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Exertional syncope, particularly with a family history of sudden cardiac death.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young competitive athletes?
cards.a: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a major cause, although other structural and electrical disorders can also cause sudden death.

cards.q: What is the classic ECG finding associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Left ventricular hypertrophy, often with repolarization abnormalities and sometimes deep narrow Q waves.

cards.q: What congenital cardiac lesion causes right ventricular volume overload?
cards.a: A significant atrial septal defect (ASD) causes chronic left-to-right flow into the right atrium and ventricle.

cards.q: What is the characteristic ECG finding in an ostium secundum ASD?
cards.a: Incomplete right bundle branch block with right ventricular conduction/volume-overload findings may occur.

cards.q: What is the most common type of ASD?
cards.a: Ostium secundum ASD.

cards.q: What is the classic complication of an unrepaired large ASD in adulthood?
cards.a:
Pulmonary hypertension and eventual Eisenmenger syndrome, although this typically develops later than with some other large shunts.
PEDIATRIC PULMONOLOGY

cards.q: What is the most common cause of respiratory distress syndrome in premature infants?
cards.a: Pulmonary surfactant deficiency due to immature type II pneumocytes.

cards.q: What is the main function of surfactant protein and phospholipid in the alveoli?
cards.a: They reduce surface tension, increasing lung compliance and preventing alveolar collapse.

cards.q: Which fetal hormone accelerates pulmonary surfactant production?
cards.a: Cortisol promotes fetal lung maturation and surfactant production.

cards.q: What antenatal medication is used to reduce neonatal respiratory morbidity when preterm delivery is anticipated?
cards.a: Betamethasone or dexamethasone given antenatally when indicated.

cards.q: What is a major complication of respiratory distress syndrome in premature infants?
cards.a: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), especially in extremely premature infants requiring prolonged respiratory support.

cards.q: What is the classic clinical definition of bronchopulmonary dysplasia?
cards.a: Chronic respiratory disease in a premature infant requiring ongoing oxygen or respiratory support beyond the expected period of acute respiratory illness, with definitions varying by gestational age and contemporary criteria.

cards.q: What is the classic chest x-ray appearance of bronchopulmonary dysplasia?
cards.a: Heterogeneous areas of hyperinflation and atelectasis with interstitial changes in established disease.

cards.q: What is a major long-term respiratory complication of extreme prematurity?
cards.a: Chronic lung disease/bronchopulmonary dysplasia, with increased susceptibility to respiratory infections and wheezing.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pulmonary edema due to congenital heart disease?
cards.a: Tachypnea, increased work of breathing, feeding difficulty, crackles, hepatomegaly, and poor weight gain.

cards.q: Why does pulmonary edema occur with a significant left-to-right cardiac shunt?
cards.a: Excessive pulmonary blood flow increases pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, promoting fluid movement into the interstitium and alveoli.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pleural effusion associated with bacterial pneumonia?
cards.a: Persistent fever, respiratory distress, pleuritic chest pain, and decreased breath sounds despite appropriate treatment.

cards.q: What is the preferred imaging study for detecting a complicated parapneumonic effusion?
cards.a: Chest ultrasound is highly useful for identifying and characterizing pleural fluid and septations.

cards.q: What is an empyema?
cards.a: Infected purulent fluid within the pleural space, usually occurring as a complication of bacterial pneumonia.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a pulmonary abscess in a child?
cards.a: Persistent fever, cough, systemic illness, and a cavitary lung lesion, often following aspiration or severe bacterial infection.

cards.q: What is the most important initial management principle for a child with severe respiratory distress?
cards.a: Rapidly assess and support airway, breathing, and circulation, while providing supplemental oxygen and escalating respiratory support as needed.

cards.q: What clinical finding indicates impending respiratory failure in a child?
cards.a: Altered mental status, exhaustion, apnea, severe hypoxemia despite oxygen, poor respiratory effort, or bradycardia indicates impending respiratory failure and requires immediate escalation of support.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) on abdominal examination?
cards.a: Abdominal distention, tenderness, decreased bowel sounds, and sometimes abdominal wall erythema or discoloration in a sick premature infant.

cards.q: What radiographic finding in NEC suggests intestinal perforation?
cards.a: Pneumoperitoneum (free intraperitoneal air).

cards.q: What is the major surgical indication in necrotizing enterocolitis?
cards.a: Intestinal perforation, or clinical deterioration despite maximal medical therapy with evidence of necrotic bowel.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of spontaneous intestinal perforation in a very premature infant?
cards.a: Sudden abdominal distention and clinical deterioration, often with free intraperitoneal air, but without the classic pneumatosis of NEC.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH)?
cards.a: A newborn with severe respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen, decreased breath sounds on the affected side, and bowel sounds in the chest.

cards.q: Which side is most commonly affected by congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
cards.a: The left side (Bochdalek hernia) is most common.

cards.q: What is the primary respiratory problem in congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
cards.a: Pulmonary hypoplasia with associated pulmonary hypertension due to compression of developing lungs.

cards.q: What is an important initial management principle for a newborn with CDH?
cards.a: Avoid bag-mask ventilation because it can inflate herniated bowel and worsen pulmonary compression; use endotracheal intubation and gastric decompression.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of esophageal atresia without a distal tracheoesophageal fistula?
cards.a: Excessive secretions, choking/cyanosis, and inability to pass an orogastric tube, with little or no gas in the abdomen.

cards.q: What prenatal finding strongly suggests esophageal atresia?
cards.a: Polyhydramnios due to impaired fetal swallowing.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of congenital diaphragmatic hernia on prenatal ultrasound?
cards.a: Abdominal organs, particularly bowel, visualized within the thoracic cavity, often with mediastinal shift.

cards.q: What is the major vascular complication of severe portal hypertension in a child?
cards.a: Esophageal varices, which can cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of esophageal variceal bleeding?
cards.a: Sudden, painless hematemesis in a child with portal hypertension or chronic liver disease.

cards.q: What is the initial priority in a child with massive variceal hemorrhage?
cards.a: Airway protection and hemodynamic stabilization, followed by urgent endoscopic therapy.

cards.q: What is the preferred endoscopic treatment for esophageal variceal bleeding?
cards.a: Endoscopic variceal ligation when technically feasible.

cards.q: What is a major cause of portal hypertension in children worldwide?
cards.a:
Chronic liver disease/cirrhosis is an important cause; extrahepatic portal vein obstruction is also a major pediatric cause in some settings.
PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY

cards.q: What is the most common cause of acquired heart disease following an upper respiratory infection in children?
cards.a: Acute rheumatic fever can follow untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

cards.q: How long after streptococcal pharyngitis does acute rheumatic fever typically occur?
cards.a: Usually 2–4 weeks after the infection.

cards.q: What diagnostic framework is used for acute rheumatic fever?
cards.a: The Jones criteria, requiring evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection plus the appropriate combination of major and minor criteria.

cards.q: What are the major Jones criteria?
cards.a: Carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules.

cards.q: What is Sydenham chorea?
cards.a: A delayed neurologic manifestation of rheumatic fever characterized by involuntary, purposeless movements, emotional lability, and motor incoordination.

cards.q: What type of arthritis is characteristic of acute rheumatic fever?
cards.a: Migratory polyarthritis, typically involving large joints.

cards.q: What is the classic skin lesion of acute rheumatic fever?
cards.a: Erythema marginatum—a nonpruritic, serpiginous, erythematous rash mainly on the trunk and proximal extremities.

cards.q: What is the classic congenital cardiac lesion associated with fetal alcohol exposure?
cards.a: Atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, and other congenital heart abnormalities can occur; no single cardiac lesion is uniquely diagnostic.

cards.q: What congenital heart lesion is particularly associated with maternal rubella infection?
cards.a: Patent ductus arteriosus, along with pulmonary artery stenosis and other congenital abnormalities.

cards.q: What congenital cardiac lesion is associated with DiGeorge syndrome?
cards.a: Conotruncal abnormalities, particularly Tetralogy of Fallot and interrupted aortic arch.

cards.q: What is the classic cardiac association of Noonan syndrome?
cards.a: Pulmonary valve stenosis is the characteristic congenital heart lesion.

cards.q: What is the classic cardiac association of Marfan syndrome?
cards.a: Aortic root dilation with risk of aortic aneurysm/dissection and mitral valve prolapse.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of aortic dissection in a patient with Marfan syndrome?
cards.a: Sudden severe chest or back pain, potentially accompanied by pulse or blood-pressure asymmetry and hemodynamic instability.

cards.q: What is the characteristic murmur of mitral regurgitation?
cards.a: A holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex, often radiating toward the axilla.

cards.q: What is the characteristic murmur of mitral stenosis?
cards.a: A low-pitched diastolic rumble with an opening snap, best heard at the apex.

cards.q: What is the classic cardiac manifestation of infective endocarditis in a child?
cards.a: Fever with a new or changing murmur, sometimes accompanied by embolic or immune-mediated findings.

cards.q: What is an important risk factor for infective endocarditis in children?
cards.a: Certain congenital heart defects, prosthetic material/valves, or previous infective endocarditis increase risk.

cards.q: What organism commonly causes infective endocarditis in children with congenital heart disease?
cards.a:
Viridans group streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus are important causes, depending on the clinical setting.
PEDIATRIC PULMONOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pneumococcal pneumonia on chest x-ray?
cards.a: Lobar consolidation, although radiographic patterns can overlap among pathogens.

cards.q: What is a major complication of bacterial pneumonia in children?
cards.a: Parapneumonic effusion/empyema, lung abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, or bacteremia.

cards.q: What clinical course suggests complicated bacterial pneumonia?
cards.a: Persistent fever or respiratory distress despite appropriate antibiotics, especially with pleural fluid or worsening radiographic findings.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma?
cards.a: Gradual-onset dry cough, fever, headache, and malaise in a school-aged child or adolescent.

cards.q: What extrapulmonary manifestation can occur with Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection?
cards.a: Rash, mucositis, neurologic complications, hemolytic anemia, and other extrapulmonary manifestations can occur.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of viral croup?
cards.a: Barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor, often worse at night.

cards.q: What is the characteristic radiographic finding in croup?
cards.a: Steeple sign—subglottic narrowing on an AP neck radiograph, although imaging is usually unnecessary in typical cases.

cards.q: What distinguishes stridor from wheezing?
cards.a: Stridor generally indicates upper-airway obstruction, whereas wheezing usually reflects lower-airway narrowing.

cards.q: What does inspiratory stridor usually indicate?
cards.a: Extrathoracic upper-airway obstruction, such as laryngomalacia, croup, or epiglottitis.

cards.q: What does expiratory stridor or wheezing generally suggest?
cards.a: Intrathoracic or lower-airway obstruction, such as asthma or bronchiolitis.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of laryngomalacia?
cards.a: Chronic inspiratory stridor beginning during the first weeks of life, often worsened by feeding, crying, or supine positioning.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital cause of chronic stridor in infancy?
cards.a: Laryngomalacia.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of tracheomalacia?
cards.a: Expiratory or biphasic noisy breathing, cough, recurrent respiratory infections, and symptoms that may worsen with crying or exertion.

cards.q: What is the underlying problem in tracheomalacia?
cards.a: Excessive collapsibility of the tracheal walls due to weakness of the supporting cartilage.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of obstructive sleep apnea caused by adenotonsillar hypertrophy?
cards.a: Habitual snoring, witnessed apneas, restless sleep, mouth breathing, and daytime behavioral or learning problems.

cards.q: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea when the diagnosis requires objective confirmation?
cards.a: Overnight polysomnography (sleep study).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pyloric stenosis on physical examination?
cards.a: A palpable “olive-shaped” mass in the right upper quadrant/epigastrium, sometimes accompanied by visible gastric peristaltic waves.

cards.q: Why is vomiting in pyloric stenosis nonbilious?
cards.a: The obstruction is at the gastric outlet, proximal to the duodenum and ampulla of Vater, so bile does not enter the vomitus.

cards.q: What metabolic abnormality should be corrected before pyloromyotomy?
cards.a: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and volume depletion should be corrected before surgery.

cards.q: What is the characteristic presentation of congenital chloride diarrhea?
cards.a: Profuse watery diarrhea beginning in the neonatal period, abdominal distention, dehydration, and metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of congenital chloride diarrhea?
cards.a: Defective intestinal Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange causes excessive chloride secretion into the intestinal lumen.

cards.q: What acid-base abnormality is characteristic of congenital chloride diarrhea?
cards.a: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of congenital lactase deficiency?
cards.a: Severe watery diarrhea, abdominal distention, and dehydration beginning with the first exposure to lactose-containing feeds.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of necrotizing enterocolitis in a premature infant?
cards.a: Feeding intolerance followed by abdominal distention, bloody stools, systemic instability, and possible intestinal perforation.

cards.q: Why does NEC occur predominantly in premature infants?
cards.a: Immature intestinal defenses, abnormal microbial colonization, and intestinal ischemia contribute to intestinal mucosal injury and inflammation.

cards.q: What is the most important nutritional intervention to reduce NEC risk in premature infants?
cards.a: Human breast milk is preferred when available because it is associated with a lower risk of NEC than formula feeding.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Meckel diverticulum bleeding?
cards.a: Painless, sometimes substantial lower GI bleeding, often caused by acid-producing ectopic gastric mucosa.

cards.q: What is the "rule of 2s" historically associated with Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: Approximately 2% of the population, located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve, about 2 inches long, and may present before age 2 years. These are teaching heuristics rather than exact epidemiologic rules.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a Meckel diverticulum causing obstruction?
cards.a: Abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and intestinal obstruction, potentially from intussusception or a fibrous band.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of volvulus caused by intestinal malrotation?
cards.a: Sudden bilious vomiting with abdominal pain and rapid clinical deterioration due to possible bowel ischemia.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial management when volvulus is strongly suspected?
cards.a: Immediate surgical consultation and urgent operative management, while simultaneously stabilizing the child.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Hirschsprung disease in a neonate?
cards.a: Delayed meconium passage, abdominal distention, vomiting, and constipation, often followed by explosive stool after rectal examination.

cards.q: What is the characteristic rectal examination finding in Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: An empty rectal vault, followed by explosive passage of stool/gas after withdrawal of the examining finger.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: Surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with pull-through of normally innervated bowel.

cards.q: What is a serious complication of Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, characterized by fever, abdominal distention, diarrhea, and systemic toxicity.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of functional abdominal pain in children?
cards.a:
Chronic or recurrent abdominal pain without evidence of an organic disorder, often with normal growth and physical examination.
PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic ECG finding in atrial septal defect?
cards.a: Right-axis deviation and incomplete right bundle branch block may occur, particularly with significant right-sided volume overload.

cards.q: What is the classic auscultatory finding in ASD caused by increased pulmonary blood flow?
cards.a: A systolic ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border due to increased flow across the pulmonic valve.

cards.q: Why is the S₂ fixed and widely split in ASD?
cards.a: Persistent right ventricular volume overload causes delayed pulmonic valve closure that does not vary normally with respiration.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a large ventricular septal defect during infancy?
cards.a: Poor feeding, diaphoresis with feeds, tachypnea, recurrent respiratory infections, and failure to thrive as pulmonary vascular resistance falls.

cards.q: What happens to pulmonary vascular resistance immediately after birth?
cards.a: It falls substantially as the lungs expand and pulmonary blood flow increases.

cards.q: Why does a large VSD often become symptomatic several weeks after birth?
cards.a: The fall in pulmonary vascular resistance increases left-to-right shunting and pulmonary blood flow, producing volume overload and heart failure.

cards.q: What is the classic murmur of a PDA?
cards.a: A continuous machine-like murmur, often loudest near the left upper sternal border.

cards.q: What pulse finding is associated with a significant PDA?
cards.a: Bounding pulses with widened pulse pressure.

cards.q: What is the classic murmur of pulmonary valve stenosis?
cards.a: A crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border.

cards.q: What syndrome is strongly associated with pulmonary valve stenosis?
cards.a: Noonan syndrome.

cards.q: What is the classic physical finding in coarctation of the aorta?
cards.a: Weak or delayed femoral pulses with higher blood pressure in the arms than in the legs.

cards.q: What is the classic chest x-ray finding in longstanding coarctation?
cards.a: Inferior rib notching from enlarged collateral intercostal arteries; a "figure-3" contour may also be seen.

cards.q: Why does coarctation cause upper-extremity hypertension?
cards.a: The obstruction increases pressure proximal to the narrowed aortic segment, producing hypertension in vessels supplying the upper body.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a: Cyanosis, exertional symptoms, systolic ejection murmur, and episodic hypercyanotic spells in more severe obstruction.

cards.q: What determines the severity of cyanosis in Tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a: Primarily the degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

cards.q: Why does squatting improve exercise tolerance in children with Tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a: Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance, reducing right-to-left shunting and improving pulmonary blood flow.

cards.q: What is the classic x-ray appearance of Tetralogy of Fallot?
cards.a: A boot-shaped cardiac silhouette due largely to right ventricular hypertrophy.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of transposition of the great arteries?
cards.a: Severe neonatal cyanosis shortly after birth, often with relatively little response to supplemental oxygen.

cards.q: What anatomical arrangement produces TGA?
cards.a: Ventriculoarterial discordance: the right ventricle connects to the aorta and the left ventricle connects to the pulmonary artery.

cards.q: What is the immediate physiologic goal in a severely cyanotic newborn with suspected TGA?
cards.a:
Improve mixing of systemic and pulmonary circulations, often by maintaining ductal patency with PGE₁ and, when necessary, performing balloon atrial septostomy.
PEDIATRIC PULMONOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of neonatal transient tachypnea?
cards.a: Early respiratory distress with tachypnea, often beginning shortly after birth and resolving within approximately 1–3 days.

cards.q: What is the major pathophysiologic problem in transient tachypnea of the newborn?
cards.a: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.

cards.q: What is a major risk factor for transient tachypnea of the newborn?
cards.a: Cesarean delivery without labor, particularly at term or near term.

cards.q: What is the classic chest x-ray appearance of transient tachypnea?
cards.a: Hyperinflation with prominent pulmonary vascular markings and fluid in the interlobar fissures.

cards.q: How does neonatal respiratory distress syndrome differ from transient tachypnea radiographically?
cards.a: RDS typically shows low lung volumes and diffuse ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms, whereas TTN often shows hyperinflation and prominent vascular/interstitial markings.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome?
cards.a: Tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, cyanosis, and increasing oxygen requirement shortly after premature birth.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiologic consequence of surfactant deficiency?
cards.a: Increased alveolar surface tension causes alveolar collapse, decreased lung compliance, increased work of breathing, and impaired gas exchange.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn?
cards.a: Severe hypoxemia with relatively clear or nonspecific lung findings, caused by persistently elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and right-to-left shunting.

cards.q: What is an important treatment for severe PPHN?
cards.a: Inhaled nitric oxide can selectively reduce pulmonary vascular resistance in appropriately selected term or near-term infants.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of inhaled nitric oxide in PPHN?
cards.a:
It activates guanylate cyclase → increases cGMP → relaxes pulmonary vascular smooth muscle, reducing pulmonary vascular resistance.
NO→↑cGMP→pulmonary vasodilation

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of infantile colic?
cards.a: Recurrent episodes of excessive crying in an otherwise healthy, normally growing infant, often occurring in the evening and resolving spontaneously by about 3–4 months.

cards.q: What finding argues against infantile colic?
cards.a: Poor weight gain, fever, bilious vomiting, bloody stool, persistent abdominal distention, or an abnormal physical examination suggests an underlying disorder.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of cow's milk protein allergy?
cards.a: Infants may develop blood-streaked stools, vomiting, diarrhea, eczema, or feeding intolerance after exposure to cow's milk protein.

cards.q: What is a typical presentation of food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis?
cards.a: A well-appearing young infant with small amounts of bright-red blood and mucus in the stool, usually without systemic illness.

cards.q: What is the treatment for food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis in a breastfed infant?
cards.a: Maternal elimination of the offending protein, commonly cow's milk, while continuing breastfeeding.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES)?
cards.a: Profuse repetitive vomiting, lethargy, pallor, and sometimes diarrhea occurring hours after ingestion of a trigger food.

cards.q: How does FPIES differ from IgE-mediated food allergy?
cards.a: FPIES is generally a non-IgE-mediated gastrointestinal hypersensitivity, typically producing delayed vomiting rather than immediate urticaria or anaphylaxis.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of intussusception after a viral infection?
cards.a: An otherwise healthy child develops episodic severe abdominal pain with vomiting and lethargy, sometimes followed by bloody stool.

cards.q: Why can children with intussusception become lethargic between pain episodes?
cards.a: Intermittent visceral pain and systemic stress can produce marked lethargy, which may be an important clue even when abdominal findings are initially subtle.

cards.q: What is the first priority when a child with intussusception is hemodynamically unstable?
cards.a: Resuscitation with IV fluids and stabilization of airway/breathing/circulation before definitive reduction.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of bowel obstruction caused by adhesions in a child?
cards.a: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distention, and decreased passage of stool/flatus, especially in a child with prior abdominal surgery.

cards.q: What type of vomiting strongly suggests intestinal obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater?
cards.a: Bilious (green) vomiting.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of incarcerated bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Persistent abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, tenderness, and systemic toxicity, with concern for strangulation and ischemia.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of gastroenteritis-associated dehydration?
cards.a: Decreased urine output, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, reduced tears, and delayed capillary refill, with severity depending on the degree of fluid loss.

cards.q: Which finding is most concerning for hypovolemic shock in a dehydrated child?
cards.a:
Hypotension, because it is generally a late sign in pediatric hypovolemic shock.
PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY

cards.q: What is the most common congenital heart defect overall?
cards.a: Ventricular septal defect (VSD).

cards.q: What is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease presenting in the neonatal period?
cards.a: Transposition of the great arteries (TGA) is a major cause of profound neonatal cyanosis.

cards.q: What congenital heart lesion classically produces cyanosis that worsens during feeding or crying?
cards.a: Tetralogy of Fallot, particularly in infants with significant right ventricular outflow obstruction.

cards.q: What is the classic treatment for a hypercyanotic tet spell after positioning and oxygen?
cards.a: Morphine, IV fluids, and β-blockade such as propranolol may be used depending on severity and clinical circumstances; severe refractory cases require escalation.

cards.q: Why can morphine help during a tet spell?
cards.a: It reduces agitation and catecholamine-driven increases in right ventricular outflow obstruction.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of an atrioventricular septal defect?
cards.a: Congestive heart failure, recurrent respiratory infections, poor growth, and a characteristic murmur, especially in infants with complete AVSD.

cards.q: Which chromosomal abnormality is strongly associated with complete AVSD?
cards.a: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).

cards.q: What is the embryologic defect underlying AV septal defects?
cards.a: Abnormal development of the endocardial cushions, resulting in defects of the atrial/ventricular septa and AV valves.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Ebstein anomaly?
cards.a: Tricuspid regurgitation, right-sided heart failure, cyanosis, and arrhythmias, particularly supraventricular tachyarrhythmias.

cards.q: What is the anatomical abnormality in Ebstein anomaly?
cards.a: Apical displacement of the tricuspid valve, producing an abnormally large right atrium and "atrialized" portion of the right ventricle.

cards.q: What maternal medication exposure is associated with Ebstein anomaly?
cards.a: Lithium exposure during pregnancy is a classic association.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of truncus arteriosus?
cards.a: A newborn with cyanosis, heart failure, increased pulmonary blood flow, and a single arterial trunk supplying systemic and pulmonary circulation.

cards.q: Which congenital syndrome is associated with truncus arteriosus?
cards.a: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome) is an important association.

cards.q: What is the key anatomical feature of truncus arteriosus?
cards.a: A single arterial trunk arises from the heart and supplies systemic, pulmonary, and coronary circulation, usually accompanied by a VSD.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR)?
cards.a: Cyanosis with varying degrees of respiratory distress and heart failure, depending on whether pulmonary venous drainage is obstructed.

cards.q: Why is an atrial septal communication essential in TAPVR?
cards.a: All pulmonary venous blood returns to the right atrium, so an ASD or patent foramen ovale allows oxygenated blood to reach the systemic circulation.

cards.q: What is the classic radiographic appearance of unobstructed supracardiac TAPVR?
cards.a:
The "snowman" or "figure-of-8" appearance, usually developing after the first few months rather than immediately after birth.
PEDIATRIC PULMONOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis?
cards.a: A viral upper-respiratory prodrome followed by tachypnea, wheezing, crackles, retractions, and feeding difficulty.

cards.q: What is the major reason infants with bronchiolitis may require hospitalization?
cards.a: Hypoxemia, apnea, dehydration, or significant respiratory distress, particularly in high-risk infants.

cards.q: What is the recommended routine therapy for uncomplicated bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Supportive care, including hydration and supplemental oxygen when clinically indicated.

cards.q: Are routine antibiotics indicated for uncomplicated viral bronchiolitis?
cards.a: No. Antibiotics do not treat the viral infection and are reserved for a documented or strongly suspected bacterial co-infection.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of croup with severe upper-airway obstruction?
cards.a: Stridor at rest, significant retractions, tachypnea, agitation, and potentially hypoxemia or fatigue.

cards.q: What is the immediate medication for severe croup?
cards.a: Nebulized epinephrine plus systemic corticosteroid, with close observation and airway support as needed.

cards.q: Why does nebulized epinephrine rapidly improve severe croup?
cards.a: Its α₁-adrenergic vasoconstrictive effect reduces subglottic mucosal edema.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of epiglottitis?
cards.a: High fever, toxic appearance, drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod positioning, and inspiratory distress.

cards.q: Why should a child with suspected epiglottitis not be forced to lie down?
cards.a: Agitation or positioning changes can worsen upper-airway obstruction and precipitate complete airway collapse.

cards.q: What organism caused most classic childhood epiglottitis before widespread vaccination?
cards.a: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib).

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of bacterial tracheitis?
cards.a: High fever, toxic appearance, stridor, respiratory distress, and thick purulent airway secretions, often following viral croup.

cards.q: What is the key difference between bacterial tracheitis and viral croup?
cards.a: Bacterial tracheitis generally produces a more toxic appearance, higher fever, and purulent secretions, with potentially severe airway obstruction.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a severe asthma exacerbation?
cards.a: Marked dyspnea, tachypnea, retractions, wheezing or absent breath sounds, inability to speak normally, and hypoxemia.

cards.q: What is the first-line bronchodilator for an acute asthma exacerbation?
cards.a: Inhaled albuterol, a short-acting β₂-adrenergic agonist.

cards.q: What additional inhaled medication is commonly added for moderate-to-severe pediatric asthma exacerbations?
cards.a: Ipratropium, an inhaled anticholinergic bronchodilator.

cards.q: What systemic medication should be given early in a moderate-to-severe asthma exacerbation?
cards.a: Systemic corticosteroids, such as oral prednisone/prednisolone or IV methylprednisolone when oral therapy is not feasible.

cards.q: What is the classic indication for magnesium sulfate in acute pediatric asthma?
cards.a: Severe asthma with inadequate response to initial bronchodilator and corticosteroid therapy, particularly when significant airflow obstruction persists.

cards.q: What is the most concerning respiratory finding in a child with severe asthma?
cards.a: Decreasing wheezing accompanied by worsening respiratory effort, altered mental status, fatigue, or poor air movement—a "silent chest" may indicate impending respiratory failure.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of inflammatory bowel disease in an adolescent?
cards.a: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, growth delay, and sometimes blood in the stool; extraintestinal manifestations may also occur.

cards.q: What clinical feature favors Crohn disease over ulcerative colitis?
cards.a: Perianal disease, transmural inflammation, skip lesions, and involvement of any part of the GI tract favor Crohn disease.

cards.q: What clinical feature favors ulcerative colitis over Crohn disease?
cards.a: Continuous colonic inflammation beginning in the rectum with bloody diarrhea favors ulcerative colitis.

cards.q: What is the characteristic endoscopic appearance of Crohn disease?
cards.a: Patchy ulceration with a cobblestone appearance, reflecting areas of inflamed mucosa separated by relatively normal tissue.

cards.q: What is the characteristic histologic finding that may occur in Crohn disease?
cards.a: Noncaseating granulomas, although they are not present in every patient.

cards.q: What is the major nutritional concern in pediatric Crohn disease?
cards.a: Poor linear growth and delayed puberty due to chronic inflammation, inadequate intake, and malabsorption.

cards.q: What is the classic complication of ulcerative colitis involving the colon?
cards.a: Toxic megacolon, characterized by severe colitis with systemic toxicity and colonic dilation.

cards.q: What clinical findings suggest toxic megacolon?
cards.a: Fever, tachycardia, abdominal distention, abdominal tenderness, systemic toxicity, and marked colonic dilation.

cards.q: What is the major immediate danger of toxic megacolon?
cards.a: Colonic perforation, sepsis, and hemodynamic instability.

cards.q: What hepatobiliary disease is strongly associated with ulcerative colitis?
cards.a: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC).

cards.q: What is the classic laboratory pattern of cholestatic liver disease?
cards.a: Predominant elevation of alkaline phosphatase and γ-glutamyl transferase (GGT), often with elevated conjugated bilirubin.

cards.q: What imaging finding is characteristic of primary sclerosing cholangitis?
cards.a: Multifocal strictures and dilation of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, producing a "beaded" appearance on cholangiography.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute pancreatitis in an older child?
cards.a: Acute epigastric abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting, often with elevated serum lipase.

cards.q: Which pancreatic enzyme is generally more useful for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Serum lipase, because it remains elevated longer and is more specific than amylase.

cards.q: What are important causes of acute pancreatitis in children?
cards.a: Trauma, medications, infections, systemic disease, gallstones, metabolic disorders, and genetic causes.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of gallstone disease in an adolescent?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, often after fatty meals, with possible nausea or vomiting.

cards.q: Which pediatric population has increased risk of cholesterol gallstones?
cards.a: Children with hemolytic disorders, obesity, rapid weight loss, or certain chronic illnesses are at increased risk.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of biliary atresia?
cards.a: Persistent neonatal jaundice, pale/acholic stools, dark urine, and hepatomegaly.

cards.q: Why are pale stools important in suspected biliary atresia?
cards.a: They indicate lack of bile reaching the intestine, suggesting extrahepatic biliary obstruction.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for biliary atresia?
cards.a:
Kasai portoenterostomy, preferably performed early, followed by liver transplantation if progressive liver disease develops.
PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Kawasaki disease in the acute phase?
cards.a: Persistent fever plus bilateral conjunctival injection, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, extremity changes, and cervical lymphadenopathy.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial treatment for Kawasaki disease?
cards.a: IVIG plus aspirin, administered promptly to reduce the risk of coronary artery complications.

cards.q: Why is aspirin used in Kawasaki disease?
cards.a: It provides anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet effects, particularly important during the subacute phase.

cards.q: What is the most important cardiac complication of Kawasaki disease?
cards.a: Coronary artery aneurysm.

cards.q: What should be suspected when a child has fever for several days plus conjunctival injection, rash, oral changes, and extremity edema?
cards.a: Kawasaki disease, particularly if no alternative diagnosis explains the findings.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of myocarditis in a child?
cards.a: Fatigue, tachycardia disproportionate to fever, dyspnea, chest pain, arrhythmias, and signs of heart failure.

cards.q: What viral infection is classically associated with myocarditis?
cards.a: Coxsackie B/enteroviruses are classic associations, although many viruses can cause myocarditis.

cards.q: What ECG abnormalities can occur in myocarditis?
cards.a: Sinus tachycardia, nonspecific ST-T changes, conduction abnormalities, and arrhythmias may occur.

cards.q: What echocardiographic finding is typical of myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction?
cards.a: Global reduction in ventricular systolic function, sometimes with ventricular dilation.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pericarditis in an adolescent?
cards.a: Sharp, pleuritic chest pain that improves when sitting forward and worsens when supine.

cards.q: What ECG finding is characteristic of acute pericarditis?
cards.a: Diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression, typically without a localized coronary distribution.

cards.q: What is the major complication of pericardial effusion?
cards.a: Cardiac tamponade, which impairs ventricular filling and can cause obstructive shock.

cards.q: What clinical finding is classically associated with cardiac tamponade?
cards.a: Hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds—Beck triad—although the complete triad is not always present in children.

cards.q: What is pulsus paradoxus?
cards.a: An exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic blood pressure, classically >10 mm Hg.

cards.q: Why does cardiac tamponade cause pulsus paradoxus?
cards.a: During inspiration, increased right-sided filling shifts the interventricular septum toward the left ventricle within the constrained pericardial space, reducing LV filling and stroke volume.

cards.q: What is the definitive emergency treatment for hemodynamically significant cardiac tamponade?
cards.a: Urgent pericardial drainage, usually by pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage depending on the cause and setting.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of myocarditis-induced cardiogenic shock?
cards.a: Hypotension, tachycardia, cool extremities, weak pulses, altered mental status, oliguria, and signs of pulmonary congestion or ventricular dysfunction.

cards.q: How does cardiogenic shock differ from hypovolemic shock?
cards.a: Cardiogenic shock results from pump failure, often with pulmonary congestion and poor cardiac output despite adequate or increased intravascular volume.

cards.q: What is a key echocardiographic feature of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Asymmetric ventricular septal hypertrophy, often with dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction.

cards.q: What is the major cause of sudden death in children with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
cards.a:
Ventricular arrhythmias are a major mechanism of sudden cardiac death.
PEDIATRIC PULMONOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of cystic fibrosis in infancy?
cards.a: Meconium ileus, failure to thrive, recurrent respiratory symptoms, or pancreatic insufficiency may be presenting features.

cards.q: What is the underlying genetic defect in cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: An autosomal recessive mutation in the CFTR gene, which encodes a chloride channel involved in epithelial ion transport.

cards.q: What is the classic sweat test finding in cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: Elevated sweat chloride concentration on appropriately performed testing.

cards.q: Why is sweat chloride elevated in cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: Dysfunctional CFTR reduces chloride reabsorption in sweat ducts, resulting in abnormally salty sweat.

cards.q: What pulmonary finding is characteristic of established cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: Chronic productive cough, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, bronchiectasis, and persistent airway colonization.

cards.q: Which organism commonly chronically colonizes the airways of patients with cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major pathogen, particularly in older children and adults.

cards.q: What pancreatic complication occurs commonly in cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, causing malabsorption and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.

cards.q: What stool characteristic suggests pancreatic insufficiency in cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: Bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea) due to fat malabsorption.

cards.q: Which vitamins are particularly deficient in cystic fibrosis-associated pancreatic insufficiency?
cards.a: Vitamins A, D, E, and K because they are fat-soluble.

cards.q: What is the classic neonatal intestinal complication of cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: Meconium ileus, caused by thick, inspissated meconium obstructing the distal ileum.

cards.q: What is the classic imaging finding in Hirschsprung disease on contrast enema?
cards.a: A transition zone between a distal aganglionic, narrowed segment and a proximally dilated segment.

cards.q: What confirms the diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: Rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absence of ganglion cells, with associated hypertrophic nerve fibers.

cards.q: What is the underlying defect in Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: Failure of neural crest cells to migrate into the distal bowel, resulting in absence of enteric ganglion cells.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of anal fissure in a child?
cards.a: Painful defecation with bright-red blood on the surface of the stool or toilet paper, commonly associated with constipation.

cards.q: Where are typical anal fissures located in children?
cards.a: Usually in the posterior midline.

cards.q: What finding should raise concern for an underlying cause rather than a simple constipation-associated fissure?
cards.a: Multiple fissures, lateral fissures, recurrent fissures, or associated systemic symptoms should prompt evaluation for conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of chronic constipation in otherwise healthy children?
cards.a: Functional constipation, often beginning after painful stool passage and resulting in stool withholding.

cards.q: What behavior commonly perpetuates functional constipation?
cards.a: Voluntary stool withholding, which causes progressive rectal distention and reduced sensation.

cards.q: What is encopresis?
cards.a: Involuntary passage of stool into inappropriate locations, commonly caused by overflow around retained stool in chronic constipation.

cards.q: What is the initial treatment for fecal impaction in functional constipation?
cards.a: Disimpaction, commonly using high-dose oral polyethylene glycol or another appropriate regimen.

cards.q: What is the maintenance treatment after fecal disimpaction?
cards.a: Daily osmotic laxative therapy, adequate fiber/fluid intake, regular toilet sitting, and behavioral interventions.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a duodenal obstruction caused by annular pancreas?
cards.a: Bilious vomiting and feeding intolerance, often beginning in infancy or sometimes presenting later.

cards.q: What is the embryologic defect in annular pancreas?
cards.a: Abnormal pancreatic development produces a ring of pancreatic tissue surrounding the second portion of the duodenum.

cards.q: Which chromosomal disorder is associated with duodenal atresia?
cards.a: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).

cards.q: What is the classic abdominal x-ray finding in duodenal atresia?
cards.a: The “double-bubble” sign, representing dilation of the stomach and proximal duodenum.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of duodenal atresia?
cards.a: Bilious vomiting shortly after birth, abdominal distention that is generally limited, and feeding intolerance.

cards.q: What is the classic x-ray finding of distal intestinal obstruction from meconium ileus?
cards.a: Dilated bowel loops with a granular or “soap-bubble” appearance from mixed meconium and gas.

cards.q: What is an important association of meconium ileus?
cards.a: Cystic fibrosis.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of Meconium plug syndrome?
cards.a: Failure to pass meconium and abdominal distention in a newborn, with passage of meconium after rectal stimulation or contrast enema.

cards.q: How does meconium plug syndrome differ from Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a:
Meconium plug syndrome may resolve after passage of the plug, whereas Hirschsprung disease has persistent aganglionosis and requires definitive evaluation and treatment.
PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic clinical finding in significant aortic stenosis?
cards.a: A harsh systolic ejection murmur with an ejection click and diminished or delayed carotid upstroke in severe disease.

cards.q: What symptom in a child with aortic stenosis is particularly concerning?
cards.a: Exertional syncope or chest pain, which may indicate severe outflow obstruction.

cards.q: What is the most common congenital valvular abnormality causing aortic stenosis in children?
cards.a: A bicuspid aortic valve.

cards.q: What is the major long-term complication of a bicuspid aortic valve?
cards.a: Progressive aortic stenosis or regurgitation and dilation of the ascending aorta.

cards.q: What is the classic murmur of aortic regurgitation?
cards.a: A high-pitched, early diastolic decrescendo murmur, best heard along the left sternal border.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a child with severe aortic coarctation after ductal closure?
cards.a: Poor feeding, tachypnea, metabolic acidosis, weak lower-extremity pulses, and shock due to inadequate systemic perfusion.

cards.q: Why can neonates with critical coarctation deteriorate rapidly after birth?
cards.a: Ductus arteriosus closure removes a major source of blood flow to the descending aorta and lower body.

cards.q: What medication can temporarily stabilize a neonate with critical coarctation?
cards.a: Prostaglandin E₁ (alprostadil) to maintain ductal patency.

cards.q: What is the classic association between coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve?
cards.a: Bicuspid aortic valve commonly coexists with coarctation, reflecting associated left-sided obstructive congenital heart disease.

cards.q: What is the classic ECG finding in severe pulmonary hypertension?
cards.a: Right ventricular hypertrophy and right-axis deviation may be present.

cards.q: What is Eisenmenger syndrome?
cards.a: Reversal of a longstanding left-to-right shunt to a right-to-left shunt due to severe pulmonary vascular disease and pulmonary hypertension.

cards.q: What clinical finding indicates development of Eisenmenger physiology?
cards.a: New or worsening cyanosis and clubbing in a patient with a longstanding congenital left-to-right shunt.

cards.q: Why should closure of a large shunt lesion be avoided after irreversible Eisenmenger physiology develops?
cards.a: The pulmonary vascular resistance is severely elevated, and closure can eliminate the compensatory pathway for systemic blood flow.

cards.q: What is the classic cardiac lesion associated with Turner syndrome?
cards.a: Coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve are important associations.

cards.q: What cardiac abnormality is associated with Williams syndrome?
cards.a: Supravalvular aortic stenosis caused by elastin-related vascular abnormalities.

cards.q: What characteristic facial/behavioral condition is associated with Williams syndrome?
cards.a: A characteristic facial appearance and overly social personality, often with developmental difficulties.

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality can occur in Williams syndrome?
cards.a: Hypercalcemia, particularly in infancy.

cards.q: What cardiac lesion is associated with Holt-Oram syndrome?
cards.a: Atrial septal defect or ventricular septal defect associated with upper-limb abnormalities.

cards.q: What is the classic clinical clue to Holt-Oram syndrome?
cards.a: Radial-ray/upper-limb abnormalities combined with a congenital cardiac defect.

cards.q: What is the major cardiac manifestation of Friedreich ataxia?
cards.a:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a major cause of morbidity and mortality.
PEDIATRIC PULMONOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pulmonary aspiration in a child with swallowing dysfunction?
cards.a: Chronic cough or choking during feeds, recurrent pneumonia, wheezing, and poor weight gain.

cards.q: What lung findings suggest chronic aspiration?
cards.a: Recurrent or persistent infiltrates, often involving dependent lung regions, along with chronic cough or wheezing.

cards.q: Which children are at increased risk for aspiration pneumonia?
cards.a: Children with neuromuscular disorders, impaired swallowing, severe developmental disability, structural abnormalities, or gastroesophageal reflux with aspiration.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of foreign-body aspiration that is initially missed?
cards.a: A child may have persistent unilateral wheezing, chronic cough, recurrent pneumonia, or asymmetric breath sounds after an unwitnessed aspiration event.

cards.q: Why can a foreign body cause unilateral hyperinflation?
cards.a: A partially obstructing object may function as a ball-valve, allowing air in during inspiration but preventing adequate expiration.

cards.q: What imaging finding can suggest a radiolucent aspirated foreign body?
cards.a: Unilateral hyperinflation or air trapping, particularly on an expiratory or decubitus film.

cards.q: What is the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for suspected airway foreign body?
cards.a: Bronchoscopy.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of bronchiectasis?
cards.a: Chronic productive cough, recurrent respiratory infections, hemoptysis, and persistent abnormal lung sounds.

cards.q: What structural change defines bronchiectasis?
cards.a: Permanent dilation and destruction of the bronchial walls caused by chronic inflammation and infection.

cards.q: What imaging study best establishes the diagnosis of bronchiectasis?
cards.a:
High-resolution CT of the chest, showing dilated bronchi, lack of normal tapering, and airway-wall abnormalities.
PEDIATRIC GASTROENTEROLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in an infant?
cards.a: Regurgitation/vomiting associated with feeding, irritability, feeding refusal, poor weight gain, or respiratory symptoms when reflux is pathologic.

cards.q: How does physiologic infant reflux differ from GERD?
cards.a: Physiologic reflux occurs in otherwise healthy infants with normal growth and no significant complications; GERD causes troublesome symptoms or complications.

cards.q: What is the initial management of uncomplicated infant reflux?
cards.a: Feeding modification and avoidance of overfeeding, with continued appropriate growth monitoring; medications are not routinely indicated.

cards.q: What symptom in an infant with reflux requires evaluation for an alternative diagnosis?
cards.a: Bilious vomiting, hematemesis, projectile vomiting with dehydration, significant abdominal distention, or failure to thrive.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of eosinophilic esophagitis in a school-aged child?
cards.a: Feeding difficulty, dysphagia, food impaction, abdominal pain, or vomiting, often with a history of atopy.

cards.q: What histologic finding establishes eosinophilic esophagitis?
cards.a: Increased eosinophilic infiltration of the esophageal mucosa with characteristic endoscopic and clinical findings.

cards.q: What is a classic endoscopic appearance of eosinophilic esophagitis?
cards.a: Esophageal rings (“trachealization”), linear furrows, exudates, and mucosal edema may be seen.

cards.q: What is an important complication of untreated eosinophilic esophagitis?
cards.a: Esophageal remodeling and stricture formation, increasing the risk of food impaction.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of appendicitis in a young child?
cards.a: It may be atypical, with diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, irritability, and delayed diagnosis compared with older children.

cards.q: What is the typical migration of pain in acute appendicitis?
cards.a: Pain classically migrates from periumbilical discomfort to the right lower quadrant as parietal peritoneal inflammation develops.

cards.q: What is the classic physical examination finding in appendicitis?
cards.a: Right lower quadrant tenderness, sometimes with guarding and rebound tenderness.

cards.q: What is the most important complication of delayed appendicitis diagnosis in children?
cards.a: Appendiceal perforation with abscess formation or generalized peritonitis.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of an appendiceal abscess?
cards.a: Persistent fever, localized right lower quadrant pain, tenderness, and sometimes a palpable mass after delayed or perforated appendicitis.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of viral gastroenteritis?
cards.a: Acute vomiting and watery diarrhea, often accompanied by fever, abdominal cramps, and sick contacts.

cards.q: What is the major complication of severe pediatric gastroenteritis?
cards.a: Dehydration with electrolyte abnormalities and hypovolemic shock.

cards.q: What is the preferred fluid for oral rehydration therapy?
cards.a: A properly formulated oral rehydration solution containing glucose and electrolytes.

cards.q: Why does glucose improve intestinal sodium and water absorption during oral rehydration?
cards.a: Glucose and sodium are cotransported across the intestinal epithelium, and water follows osmotically.

cards.q: When is IV fluid resuscitation indicated in pediatric gastroenteritis?
cards.a: For severe dehydration, hypovolemic shock, altered mental status, or inability to tolerate adequate oral rehydration.

cards.q: What is the classic acid-base abnormality from severe diarrhea?
cards.a:
Normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis due to bicarbonate loss.

cards.q: Why can severe diarrhea cause hypokalemia?
cards.a:
Gastrointestinal losses cause direct potassium depletion, which can become significant with prolonged diarrhea.
PEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute rheumatic carditis?
cards.a: Tachycardia, new murmur, cardiomegaly, heart failure, or pericardial involvement following group A streptococcal infection.

cards.q: Which valve is most commonly affected by rheumatic heart disease?
cards.a: The mitral valve is most commonly affected.

cards.q: What is the characteristic chronic valvular lesion of rheumatic heart disease?
cards.a: Mitral stenosis, although mitral regurgitation is common earlier in the disease course.

cards.q: How is prevention of recurrent rheumatic fever achieved?
cards.a: Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis, typically with benzathine penicillin G at recommended intervals.

cards.q: What is the major purpose of secondary rheumatic fever prophylaxis?
cards.a: To prevent recurrent group A streptococcal infection and subsequent progressive valvular damage.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute rheumatic fever-associated chorea?
cards.a: Involuntary, irregular movements, motor incoordination, handwriting deterioration, and emotional lability.

cards.q: What is the classic ECG abnormality that counts as a minor Jones criterion?
cards.a: Prolonged PR interval, adjusted for age.

cards.q: What is the classic congenital lesion producing a continuous left-to-right shunt?
cards.a: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

cards.q: What happens to the shunt in PDA when pulmonary vascular resistance becomes very high?
cards.a: The left-to-right shunt can eventually reverse, producing Eisenmenger physiology and cyanosis.

cards.q: What is the characteristic differential cyanosis of PDA-associated Eisenmenger syndrome?
cards.a: Lower-extremity cyanosis and clubbing greater than the upper extremities, because the ductus enters the descending aorta distal to vessels supplying the upper limbs.

cards.q: Which congenital heart lesion is classically associated with differential cyanosis?
cards.a: PDA with Eisenmenger physiology.

cards.q: What is the classic murmur of a VSD?
cards.a: A harsh, holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border.

cards.q: Why can a small VSD have a louder murmur than a large VSD?
cards.a: A small defect produces higher-velocity turbulent flow, generating a louder murmur.

cards.q: Why can the murmur of a large VSD become softer as pulmonary vascular resistance rises?
cards.a: Increasing pulmonary vascular resistance reduces the pressure gradient across the VSD and decreases shunt velocity.

cards.q: What is the classic ECG finding in a significant ASD?
cards.a: Right ventricular volume overload, often manifested by incomplete RBBB and right-axis deviation depending on the defect and age.

cards.q: What is the usual direction of blood flow through an uncomplicated ASD?
cards.a: Left-to-right, because left atrial pressure normally exceeds right atrial pressure.

cards.q: What is the classic congenital cardiac lesion associated with an "egg-on-a-string" appearance?
cards.a: Transposition of the great arteries, particularly on older radiographs.

cards.q: Why is TGA incompatible with life without mixing?
cards.a: The systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel rather than in series, so oxygenated blood cannot adequately reach the systemic circulation without an effective mixing site.

cards.q: What are important sites of mixing in TGA?
cards.a: Atrial-level communication, VSD, and PDA can permit mixing between the parallel circulations.

cards.q: What is the definitive surgical repair for TGA?
cards.a:
Arterial switch operation, generally performed early in life.
PEDIATRIC PULMONOLOGY

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pulmonary tuberculosis in a child?
cards.a: Persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss or poor weight gain, with possible lymphadenopathy or pulmonary findings.

cards.q: What is the preferred initial test for TB infection in an immunocompetent child?
cards.a: Tuberculin skin testing or an interferon-γ release assay (IGRA), depending on age, vaccination history, and clinical circumstances.

cards.q: What is the classic chest x-ray finding of primary pulmonary TB in children?
cards.a: Hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy, sometimes with an associated parenchymal focus.

cards.q: Why can TB cause airway obstruction in children?
cards.a: Enlarged hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes can compress adjacent bronchi.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of pertussis?
cards.a: Paroxysmal coughing fits, inspiratory whoop, and posttussive vomiting; young infants may present primarily with apnea.

cards.q: Which organism causes pertussis?
cards.a: Bordetella pertussis.

cards.q: What is the major danger of pertussis in young infants?
cards.a: Apnea, hypoxemia, pneumonia, and severe respiratory compromise.

cards.q: What is the classic laboratory finding during the catarrhal/paroxysmal phase of pertussis?
cards.a: Marked lymphocytosis, particularly in young infants.

cards.q: What antibiotic is preferred for treatment and transmission reduction in pertussis?
cards.a: A macrolide, usually azithromycin, is preferred.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a pulmonary infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis in an infant?
cards.a: Afebrile pneumonia with a staccato cough, tachypnea, and diffuse interstitial infiltrates, typically occurring at several weeks of age.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a choledochal cyst in a child?
cards.a: Abdominal pain, jaundice, and a palpable abdominal mass may occur, although the classic triad is uncommon.

cards.q: What is the major complication of a choledochal cyst?
cards.a: Cholangitis, pancreatitis, biliary obstruction, and increased lifetime risk of biliary malignancy.

cards.q: What imaging study is commonly used to evaluate suspected choledochal cysts?
cards.a: Abdominal ultrasound is a useful initial study; MRCP can further define biliary anatomy.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute cholangitis?
cards.a: Fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice (Charcot triad).

cards.q: What additional findings suggest severe ascending cholangitis?
cards.a: Hypotension and altered mental status indicate severe systemic illness.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant pain, fever, nausea/vomiting, and a positive Murphy sign.

cards.q: What is Murphy sign?
cards.a: Inspiratory arrest caused by pain when the examiner palpates the right upper quadrant over the gallbladder.

cards.q: What is the classic ultrasound finding of acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, gallstones, and a sonographic Murphy sign may be present.

cards.q: What is the classic presentation of appendicitis-associated perforation?
cards.a: Persistent fever, worsening abdominal pain, guarding, rebound tenderness, and systemic toxicity.
